findings.claim: FASB ASU 2014-09 (Topic 606), the five-step revenue-recognition model (Source: OpenStax, Accounting Vol 1, Ch 9.1), is the canonical SaaS revenue-recognition framework.
findings.failure_mode: software-industry claim attached to a source citation; source disclaims the depth
findings.evidence: Deep 274-284 gives the five steps and the principle-based replacement; neither deep nor source mentions SaaS or software revenue. Source 23749-23750 (Ch 9.1): 'a detailed look at each of these five requirements is too involved for an introductory course'.
findings.fix: correct: FASB ASU 2014-09 (Topic 606), the five-step revenue-recognition model (Ch 9.1), is the principle-based framework that governs when contract revenue is recognised, including for software contracts. The book introduces the five steps only; it calls a detailed treatment 'too involved for an introductory course'.

findings.claim: SOX 302 ... and SOX 404 ... make security, reliability, and change-management investment a personally-certified line. Investment in audit-trail integrity, segregation of duties, and access controls is no longer a discretionary engineering preference; it is a financial-statement-attestation requirement.
findings.failure_mode: scope of SOX attestation widened beyond internal control over financial reporting
findings.evidence: Deep 239-240: Section 404 covers annual audits of internal control effectiveness; Section 302 certifies the internal control report and fair statement of financial condition. Source 21796-21797: 404 covers 'all internal controls that have an impact on the financial reporting of the organization'. Nothing extends certification to reliability or change-management investment generally.
findings.fix: correct: SOX 302 and 404 make internal controls that bear on financial reporting a personally certified line; where audit trails, segregation of duties and access controls touch financial reporting, they are an attestation requirement, not an engineering preference.

findings.claim: Modern SOX compliance has expanded into cybersecurity disclosure (Source: Ch 8.7), so a software business's data-breach posture is now a SOX-attested concern.

findings.fix: correct: Cybersecurity is one of the conditions increasingly affecting SOX compliance, and SOX guidelines now allow application to IT activities (Ch 8.7), so data-breach posture is moving into SOX scope.

notes: Drift concentrates in one root cause: the distillation imports US software-accounting practice from outside the source (ASC 350-40 internal-use-software capitalisation with preliminary-project and application-development stages; ASC 606 standalone-selling-price allocation, residual method, stand-ready obligations; bookings-to-billings; MD&A as the disclosure mechanism) and in several places attaches Ch 9.1 or Ch 11.x citations to it. The source never discusses software or SaaS revenue, and says the five-step model's detail is 'too involved for an introductory course' (source 23749-23750); that limit belongs in Named limits and in the deep ref. 'Going-concern' is misused four times (lines 16, 104, 146, 173) to mean auditor-independence failure. Faithful core: COSO components and six internal-control elements, SOX 302/404 content, penalties and retention, fraud triangle, burn rate, contingent-liability matrix and range rule, audit-committee and rotation facts, Waste Management $1.7B, Enron $40B. Integration rows for Accounting Vol 2, Principles of Finance, Business Law, Principles of Management, Jones and Letaw check out against their deep refs; Marketing's 'customer journey' and the Business Ethics front-page claim do not.
